claim: HIV-1 Vif is able to degrade the PPP2R5 family of regulatory subunits of key cellular phosphatase PP2A (PPP2R5A-E).
source: We recently reported that HIV-1 Vif is also able to degrade the PPP2R5 family of regulatory subunits of key cellular phosphatase PP2A (PPP2R5A-E; Greenwood et al., 2016; Naamati et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Greenwood et al., 2016; Naamati et al., 2019).

claim: Amino acid polymorphisms at positions 31 and 128 of HIV-1 Vif selectively regulate the degradation of PPP2R5 family proteins.
source: We now identify amino acid polymorphisms at positions 31 and 128 of HIV-1 Vif which selectively regulate the degradation of PPP2R5 family proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including flow cytometry and proteomic analyses.

claim: Residues 31 and 128 of HIV-1 Vif covary across HIV-1 viruses in vivo, favouring depletion of PPP2R5A-E.
source: These residues covary across HIV-1 viruses in vivo, favouring depletion of PPP2R5A-E.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of naturally occurring HIV-1 Vif sequences and statistical tests showing significant covariance.

claim: Degradation of PPP2R5 family subunits is both necessary and sufficient for Vif-dependent G2/M cell cycle arrest.
source: Through analysis of point mutants and naturally occurring Vif variants, we further show that degradation of PPP2R5 family subunits is both necessary and sufficient for Vif-dependent G2/M cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from point mutants, siRNA knockdowns, and cell cycle analysis.

claim: Antagonism of PP2A by HIV-1 Vif is independent of APOBEC3 family proteins.
source: Antagonism of PP2A by HIV-1 Vif is therefore independent of APOBEC3 family proteins, and regulates cell cycle progression in HIV-infected cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that Vif mutants can separate PPP2R5 and APOBEC3 family protein depletion.

claim: The canonical function of HIV-1 Vif is to recruit the cellular restriction factor APOBEC3G for CUL5 E3 ligase and ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent degradation in infected cells.
source: The canonical function of HIV-1 Vif is to recruit the cellular restriction factor APOBEC3G for CUL5 E3 ligase and ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent degradation in infected cells, preventing APOBEC3G encapsidation and enhancing virion infectivity (Conticello et al., 2003; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Marin et al., 2003; Mehle et al., 2004; Sheehy et al., 2002; Sheehy et al., 2003; Stopak et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The ability of Vif to antagonise APOBEC3G and its homologues is broadly conserved across lentiviral phylogeny.
source: This interaction is very likely to be important in vivo, because the ability of Vif to antagonise APOBEC3G and its homologues is broadly conserved across lentiviral phylogeny, and has driven co-evolution of the mammalian APOBEC3 family (Compton et al., 2013; Nakano et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on lentiviral phylogeny and APOBEC3 co-evolution.

claim: Vif induces G2/M cell cycle arrest in multiple studies.
source: The other cell biological phenotype associated with Vif in multiple studies is the induction of G2/M cell cycle arrest (DeHart et al., 2008; Evans et al., 2018; Izumi et al., 2010; Sakai et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest does not require expression of APOBEC3 family proteins.
source: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest does not require expression of APOBEC3 family proteins, but is reliant on lysine-48 ubiquitination and the same CUL5 E3 ligase complex recruited by Vif to deplete APOBEC3G (DeHart et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest is suspected to reflect ubiquitination and degradation of an unknown cellular factor involved in cell cycle progression.
source: It has therefore been suspected to reflect ubiquitination and degradation of an unknown cellular factor involved in cell cycle progression (DeHart et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous work cited.

claim: Only certain HIV-1 Vif variants mediate cell cycle arrest.
source: Why only certain HIV-1 Vif variants mediate this effect (Evans et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015), and how widely conserved it is across the lentiviral lineage, have remained unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing variability among Vif variants.

claim: Vif is able to degrade the B56 family of regulatory subunits of PP2A (PPP2R5A-E) in HIV-1-infected CEM-T4 T cells.
source: We have recently discovered that, in addition to APOBEC3 family proteins, Vif is also able to degrade the B56 family of regulatory subunits of the ubiquitous heterotrimeric serine-threonine phosphatase PP2A (PPP2R5A-E) in HIV-1-infected CEM-T4 T cells (Greenwood et al., 2016) and primary human CD4+ T cells (Naamati et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vif is able to degrade the B56 family of regulatory subunits of PP2A (PPP2R5A-E) in primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: We have recently discovered that, in addition to APOBEC3 family proteins, Vif is also able to degrade the B56 family of regulatory subunits of the ubiquitous heterotrimeric serine-threonine phosphatase PP2A (PPP2R5A-E) in HIV-1-infected CEM-T4 T cells (Greenwood et al., 2016) and primary human CD4+ T cells (Naamati et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PP2A is one of the major cellular serine-threonine phosphatases together with PP1.
source: Together with PP1, PP2A is one of the major cellular serine-threonine phosphatases (Nasa and Kettenbach, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: Specificity of the PP2A holoenzyme is determined by the bound regulatory subunit.
source: Specificity of the PP2A holoenzyme is determined by the bound regulatory subunit, and targets of PP2A-B56 have been implicated in a host of cellular processes, including the regulation of mitotic kinases and cell cycle progression (Foley et al., 2011; Grallert et al., 2015; Vallardi et al., 2019; Yang and Phiel, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established knowledge.

claim: Targets of PP2A-B56 have been implicated in the regulation of mitotic kinases and cell cycle progression.
source: Specificity of the PP2A holoenzyme is determined by the bound regulatory subunit, and targets of PP2A-B56 have been implicated in a host of cellular processes, including the regulation of mitotic kinases and cell cycle progression (Foley et al., 2011; Grallert et al., 2015; Vallardi et al., 2019; Yang and Phiel, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established knowledge.

claim: The ability of Vif to degrade PPP2R5 subunits is shared by Vif variants from diverse primate and non-primate lentiviruses.
source: The ability of Vif to degrade PPP2R5 subunits (illustrated for PPP2R5D in Figure 1A) is shared by Vif variants from diverse primate and non-primate lentiviruses (Greenwood et al., 2016), suggesting a beneficial effect on viral replication in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The ability of Vif to degrade PPP2R5 subunits suggests a beneficial effect on viral replication in vivo.
source: The ability of Vif to degrade PPP2R5 subunits (illustrated for PPP2R5D in Figure 1A) is shared by Vif variants from diverse primate and non-primate lentiviruses (Greenwood et al., 2016), suggesting a beneficial effect on viral replication in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the conservation of the function across lentiviruses.

claim: Depletion of PPP2R5A-E by Vif could be dependent on or secondary to the phylogenetically conserved ability of Vif to antagonise APOBEC3 family proteins.
source: In theory, however, depletion of PPP2R5A-E could be dependent on or secondary to the phylogenetically conserved ability of Vif to antagonise APOBEC3 family proteins.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presenting a theoretical possibility.

claim: Amino acid substitutions at residues 31 and 128 clearly separate APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family protein depletion.
source: To demonstrate that these functions are autonomous and have therefore been independently selected, we now screen a library of rationally designed Vif point mutants, and identify amino acid substitutions at residues 31 and 128 which clearly separate APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family protein depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the mutant screen.

claim: Antagonism of PP2A explains the ability of Vif to cause cell cycle arrest.
source: We further show that antagonism of PP2A explains the ability of Vif to cause cell cycle arrest, and that this requires efficient depletion of all PPP2R5 family subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell cycle analysis and siRNA knockdowns.

claim: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest requires efficient depletion of all PPP2R5 family subunits.
source: We further show that antagonism of PP2A explains the ability of Vif to cause cell cycle arrest, and that this requires efficient depletion of all PPP2R5 family subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdowns showing that depletion of all subunits is necessary.

claim: Naturally occurring polymorphisms of residues 31 and 128 correlate with the ability of HIV-1 Vif variants to cause cell cycle arrest.
source: Naturally occurring polymorphisms of residues 31 and 128 correlate with the ability of HIV-1 Vif variants to cause cell cycle arrest, and reveal evidence of selection pressure for PPP2R5A-E depletion in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from naturally occurring Vif variants and bioinformatic analysis.

claim: There is evidence of selection pressure for PPP2R5A-E depletion in vivo.
source: Naturally occurring polymorphisms of residues 31 and 128 correlate with the ability of HIV-1 Vif variants to cause cell cycle arrest, and reveal evidence of selection pressure for PPP2R5A-E depletion in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis showing covariance of residues 31 and 128.

claim: Vif point mutant R15A is defective for APOBEC3F depletion.
source: As previously reported (Letko et al., 2015; Nakashima et al., 2016), mutation of R15 resulted in loss of activity against APOBEC3F.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Vif point mutant RK33/34AA is partially impaired for APOBEC3F depletion.
source: The RK33/34AA mutant was also partially impaired, but other mutants retained full activity against APOBEC3F.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Vif point mutant I128A shows a partial rescue of PPP2R5D levels.
source: Interestingly, the I128A (lane 4) and Y44A (lane 9) mutations only showed a partial rescue, suggesting a differential effect on different PPP2R5 subunits (PPP2R5B vs PPP2R5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Vif point mutant Y44A shows a partial rescue of PPP2R5D levels.
source: Interestingly, the I128A (lane 4) and Y44A (lane 9) mutations only showed a partial rescue, suggesting a differential effect on different PPP2R5 subunits (PPP2R5B vs PPP2R5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Vif point mutants RK33/34AA are associated with lower levels of Vif expression.
source: In addition, mutations in residues R33/K34 (lanes 7–8) were associated with lower levels of Vif expression (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutations in residues 128 and 31 separate PPP2R5 and APOBEC3 family depletion without affecting Vif stability.
source: In conclusion, therefore, mutations in residues 128 and 31 separate PPP2R5 and APOBEC3 family depletion without affecting Vif stability, and differentially regulate the 5 PPP2R5 family members.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry, immunoblots, and proteomics.

claim: Mutations in residues 128 and 31 differentially regulate the 5 PPP2R5 family members.
source: In conclusion, therefore, mutations in residues 128 and 31 separate PPP2R5 and APOBEC3 family depletion without affecting Vif stability, and differentially regulate the 5 PPP2R5 family members.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data showing differential effects on PPP2R5A vs PPP2R5C-E.

claim: Vif point mutants F39A and D61A retain the ability to antagonise PPP2RB and cause cell cycle arrest.
source: As a control, two other Vif mutants (F39A and D61A) which retained the ability to antagonise PPP2RB (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), also retained the ability to cause cell cycle arrest (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vif point mutants I128A and I128D are unable to mediate cell cycle arrest despite retaining the ability to deplete FMR1 and DPH7.
source: Both I128A and I128D point mutants retain the ability to deplete these proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), but are unable to mediate cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from Figure 3C-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Depletion of PPP2R5 family subunits, but not other Vif substrates, is required for Vif-dependent aurora kinase activation and G2/M cell cycle arrest.
source: Depletion of PPP2R5 family subunits, but not other Vif substrates, is therefore required for Vif-dependent aurora kinase activation and G2/M cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutants defective for PPP2R5 depletion but not FMR1/DPH7 depletion fail to cause cell cycle arrest.

claim: Inhibition of PP2A with okadaic acid causes G2/M cell cycle arrest in CEM-T4s.
source: Consistent with PPP2R5A-E depletion by Vif, inhibition of PP2A with okadaic acid causes G2/M cell cycle arrest in CEM-T4s (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of WT NL4-3 Vif in HeLa cells causes cell cycle arrest.
source: First, we confirmed that, as in CEM-T4s, expression of WT NL4-3 Vif in HeLas causes cell cycle arrest (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of PPP2R5B is neither sufficient nor required for cell cycle arrest in HeLa cells.
source: That depletion of PPP2R5B is neither sufficient (Figure 4A–B) nor required (Figure 4C–D) in this setting may reflect low expression of PPP2R5B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), consistent with previous protein-level data from HeLas (Geiger et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4A-D and mRNA expression data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Transfection of a pool of siRNA targeting PPP2R5A, C, D and E (but not B) causes cell cycle arrest in wildtype HeLa cells but not HeLa cells over-expressing PPP2R5B.
source: As predicted, transfection of a pool of siRNA targeting PPP2R5A, C D and E (but not B) caused cell cycle arrest in wildtype HeLas, but not HeLas over-expressing PPP2R5B (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–E, compare with Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Knockdown of FMR1 and DPH7 does not cause cell cycle arrest.
source: Finally, knockdown of FMR1 and DPH7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) did not cause cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Efficient depletion of all PPP2R5 subunits is required to cause cell cycle arrest.
source: Taken together, these observations therefore explain why efficient depletion of all PPP2R5 subunits is required to cause cell cycle arrest, and why Vif variants with impaired activity against any PPP2R5 subunit are defective for this phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdowns and Vif mutant analysis.

claim: The ability to cause G2/M cell cycle arrest varies between naturally occurring HIV-1 Vif variants.
source: The ability to cause G2/M cell cycle arrest is known to vary between naturally occurring HIV-1 Vif variants from clade B viruses (such as NL4-3 and HXB2), as well as viruses from other clades (Evans et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Substitution R33K is well tolerated for PPP2R5B depletion by NL4-3 Vif.
source: Likewise, R33K, but not R33G, was well tolerated.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HXB2, YU2 and CH470 Vif variants retain the ability to deplete APOBEC3G.
source: Depletion of APOBEC3G was preserved in each case (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Naturally occurring polymorphisms at residues 31 and 128 modulate the ability of Vif to deplete PPP2R5 family subunits.
source: Naturally occurring polymorphisms at residues 31 and 128 therefore modulate the ability of Vif to deplete PPP2R5 family subunits, and explain why some HIV-1 Vif variants are unable to cause cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from naturally occurring Vif variants.

claim: Naturally occurring polymorphisms at residues 31 and 128 explain why some HIV-1 Vif variants are unable to cause cell cycle arrest.
source: Naturally occurring polymorphisms at residues 31 and 128 therefore modulate the ability of Vif to deplete PPP2R5 family subunits, and explain why some HIV-1 Vif variants are unable to cause cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from naturally occurring Vif variants.

claim: Only ΔVpr-Vif WT virus, but not ΔVpr-ΔVif or ΔVpr-Vif AYR viruses, is able to induce G2/M cell cycle arrest in primary human CD4+ T cells.
source: A similar effect was observed in HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: The association between polymorphisms at residues 31 and 128 is statistically significant (p=0.0003).
source: Whist this difference appears modest, the association between these polymorphisms is highly statistically significant (p=0.0003, Fisher's exact test, Figure 7—figure supplement 3A, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There is significant in vivo selection pressure to maintain the ability of Vif to antagonise PP2A.
source: Taken together, these data therefore provide evidence of a functional interaction between residues 31/128, and suggest significant in vivo selection pressure to maintain the ability of Vif to antagonise PP2A.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the covariance analysis and phylogenetic data.

claim: Depletion of PPP2R5 family subunits by Vif is separable from targeting of APOBEC3 family proteins.
source: By demonstrating that depletion of PPP2R5 family subunits by Vif is separable from targeting of APOBEC3 family proteins, we formally prove that PP2A antagonism is neither required for, nor an epiphenomenon of, APOBEC3 family protein depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Vif mutants that separate these functions.

claim: PP2A antagonism by Vif is neither required for, nor an epiphenomenon of, APOBEC3 family protein depletion.
source: By demonstrating that depletion of PPP2R5 family subunits by Vif is separable from targeting of APOBEC3 family proteins, we formally prove that PP2A antagonism is neither required for, nor an epiphenomenon of, APOBEC3 family protein depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Vif mutants that separate these functions.

claim: Conservation of PPP2R5 depletion across HIV-1 viruses and the broader lentiviral lineage provides strong genetic evidence for the importance of PPP2R5 depletion by Vif in vivo.
source: Combined with evidence of conservation across HIV-1 viruses and the broader lentiviral lineage (Greenwood et al., 2016), these observations provide strong genetic evidence for the importance of PPP2R5 depletion by Vif in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from conservation data and experimental results.

claim: Residues 31, 33, and 44 of Vif are important for Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest.
source: Strikingly, the critical residues for PPP2R5 depletion identified in our screen included several previously determined to be important for Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest in other, independent studies (31, 33, 44) (DeHart et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and data from the current study.

claim: Efficient depletion of all PPP2R5 subunits is required to halt cell cycle progression.
source: In fact, because efficient depletion of all PPP2R5 subunits is required to halt cell cycle progression, these are not paradoxes at all.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdowns.

claim: Expression of HIV-1 Vif in mouse or COS cells results in depletion of PPP2R5D but does not cause cell cycle arrest.
source: First, expression of HIV-1 Vif in mouse or COS cells results in depletion of PPP2R5D, but does not cause cell cycle arrest (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In species-mismatched cells, another PPP2R5 subunit likely escapes depletion by Vif.
source: As with Vif point mutants and naturally occurring variants in human cells, it seems likely that another PPP2R5 subunit escapes depletion in these species-mismatched cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the requirement for depletion of all subunits.

claim: The ability of Vif to antagonise at least some PPP2R5 subunits is widely conserved.
source: Second, we previously found the ability of Vif to antagonise at least some PPP2R5 subunits to be widely conserved (Greenwood et al., 2016), but the ability to cause cell cycle arrest is variable amongst HIV-1 Vif variants (Evans et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The ability to cause cell cycle arrest is variable amongst HIV-1 Vif variants.
source: Second, we previously found the ability of Vif to antagonise at least some PPP2R5 subunits to be widely conserved (Greenwood et al., 2016), but the ability to cause cell cycle arrest is variable amongst HIV-1 Vif variants (Evans et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Escape of even a single PPP2R5 subunit allows cell cycle to progress.
source: Since efficient depletion of all expressed PPP2R5 subunits is required to cause cell cycle arrest, escape of even a single subunit allows cell cycle to progress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing the requirement for depletion of all subunits.

claim: The commonest single combination of residues at positions 31 and 128 among HIV-1 Vif sequences is 31I/128I, accounting for approximately 30% of Vif variants.
source: Amongst all HIV-1 Vif sequences analysed here, the commonest single combination of residues at positions 31 and 128 was 31I/128I, accounting for approximately 30% of Vif variants.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of HIV-1 Vif sequences.

claim: Most HIV-1 Vif variants with 31I/128I are expected to efficiently degrade PPP2R5A-E and cause cell cycle arrest.
source: Most of these sequences also encode 33R or 33K and, like NL4-3 and CH470 Vif, are therefore expected to efficiently degrade PPP2R5A-E, and cause cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data on NL4-3 and CH470 Vif.

claim: Only approximately 5% of HIV-1 Vif variants encode 31V/128R and are expected to be severely impaired for PPP2R5A-E degradation.
source: Conversely, only approximately 5% encode 31V/128R, and are therefore expected to be severely impaired for PPP2R5A-E degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of HIV-1 Vif sequences.

claim: Most remaining HIV-1 Vif variants are likely active against at least some PPP2R5 family members but may be variably attenuated in their ability to cause cell cycle arrest.
source: It is likely that most of the remaining Vif variants, like YU2 and HXB2, are active against at least some PPP2R5 family members, but may be variably attenuated in their ability to cause cell cycle arrest.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data on YU2 and HXB2 Vif.

claim: Naturally occurring Vif variants exhibit a spectrum of activity against APOBEC3 family proteins.
source: Interestingly, naturally occurring Vif variants have also been shown to exhibit a spectrum of activity against APOBEC3 family proteins, including variants which fail to neutralise one or more APOBEC3 family proteins (Binka et al., 2012; Iwabu et al., 2010; Mulder et al., 2008; Simon et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of aurora kinase substrates is expected to contribute significantly to Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest.
source: Mechanistically, hyperphosphorylation of aurora kinase substrates is expected to contribute significantly to Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest (Foley et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established knowledge cited.

claim: PP2A is a 'master regulator' of cell cycle.
source: Nonetheless, PP2A is a 'master regulator' of cell cycle (Wlodarchak and Xing, 2016), and depletion of PPP2R5A-E by Vif causes widespread remodelling of the phosphoproteome, implying activation of multiple kinases (Greenwood et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: Depletion of PPP2R5A-E by Vif causes widespread remodelling of the phosphoproteome, implying activation of multiple kinases.
source: Nonetheless, PP2A is a 'master regulator' of cell cycle (Wlodarchak and Xing, 2016), and depletion of PPP2R5A-E by Vif causes widespread remodelling of the phosphoproteome, implying activation of multiple kinases (Greenwood et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest requires TP53.
source: Consistent with this, Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest was previously shown to require TP53 (Izumi et al., 2010), and several studies have identified upstream regulation of TP53 by PP2A in different systems (Ajay et al., 2010; Li et al., 2002; Yang and Phiel, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several studies have identified upstream regulation of TP53 by PP2A.
source: Consistent with this, Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest was previously shown to require TP53 (Izumi et al., 2010), and several studies have identified upstream regulation of TP53 by PP2A in different systems (Ajay et al., 2010; Li et al., 2002; Yang and Phiel, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many RNA and DNA viruses cause and are thought to benefit from cell cycle arrest.
source: Many RNA and DNA viruses cause and are thought to benefit from cell cycle arrest (Bagga and Bouchard, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge.

claim: G2/M cell cycle arrest in HIV infection was first attributed to Vpr.
source: In HIV infection, G2/M cell cycle arrest was first attributed to Vpr (He et al., 1995; Jowett et al., 1995; Rogel et al., 1995), which remains better known for this function.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Early studies suggested a positive effect of G2/M arrest on transcription from the HIV-1 LTR.
source: Early studies suggested a positive effect of G2/M arrest on transcription from the HIV-1 LTR (Goh et al., 1998; Gummuluru and Emerman, 1999), but more recent results have raised the possibility that cell cycle arrest may be secondary to another Vpr-dependent process, such as antagonism of innate immunity (Laguette et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: More recent results suggest that cell cycle arrest may be secondary to another Vpr-dependent process, such as antagonism of innate immunity.
source: Early studies suggested a positive effect of G2/M arrest on transcription from the HIV-1 LTR (Goh et al., 1998; Gummuluru and Emerman, 1999), but more recent results have raised the possibility that cell cycle arrest may be secondary to another Vpr-dependent process, such as antagonism of innate immunity (Laguette et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Targeting of the same cell biological process by multiple viral accessory proteins is strong a priori evidence of biological importance in vivo.
source: Nonetheless, targeting of the same cell biological process by multiple viral accessory proteins is strong a priori evidence of biological importance in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on general reasoning about viral evolution.

claim: Functional redundancy with Vpr may help explain why Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest is not more strictly conserved across naturally occurring HIV-1 Vif variants.
source: Functional redundancy with Vpr may also help explain why Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest is not more strictly conserved across naturally occurring HIV-1 Vif variants.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presenting a possible explanation.

claim: Key polymorphic residues which regulate PPP2R5 antagonism may be subject to balancing selection pressures.
source: In addition, key polymorphic residues which regulate PPP2R5 antagonism may be subject to balancing selection pressures.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presenting a possible explanation.

claim: The requirement to maintain the Exonic Splicing Silencer of Vpr (ESSV) at the RNA level limits the sequence variability tolerated at position 128.
source: First, the requirement to maintain the Exonic Splicing Silencer of Vpr (ESSV) at the RNA level limits the sequence variability tolerated at position 128 (Madsen and Stoltzfus, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Polymorphisms at position 31 also regulate antagonism of APOBEC3H.
source: Second, polymorphisms at position 31 also regulate antagonism of APOBEC3H (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In some cases, the abilities of Vif to antagonise APOBEC3H and cause cell cycle arrest are mutually exclusive.
source: Indeed, at least in some cases, the abilities of Vif to antagonise APOBEC3H and cause cell cycle arrest were found to be mutually exclusive.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that position 31 regulates both functions.

claim: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest correlates with viral cytopathicity.
source: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest correlates with viral cytopathicity (Evans et al., 2018; Sakai et al., 2006), and was reported to enhance HIV-1 replication in vitro in a previous study using chimeric HXB2/NL4-3 Vif variants (Izumi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest was reported to enhance HIV-1 replication in vitro.
source: Vif-dependent cell cycle arrest correlates with viral cytopathicity (Evans et al., 2018; Sakai et al., 2006), and was reported to enhance HIV-1 replication in vitro in a previous study using chimeric HXB2/NL4-3 Vif variants (Izumi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Classic experiments comparing WT and Vif-deficient viruses often examined HXB2 or YU2 viruses.
source: Classic experiments comparing WT and Vif-deficient viruses in permissive cells often examined HXB2 (Gabuzda et al., 1992) or YU2 (Gaddis et al., 2003) viruses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HXB2 and YU2 Vif variants are attenuated in their activity against different PPP2R5 subunits.
